utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We see two new faces, one on each side of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, my name is Paige Petersen. I'm somewhat new to the Djordjevic team. I started in July, and this is the first time I'm leading a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Djordjevic, there's a new member of your team here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it is not a new member of our team, Your Honours. It is Ms. Jelena Dzambazovic, our case manager from the very beginning almost but she appears in the courtroom only when necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She is new to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Welcome to both of you. I think this witness is to give evidence in closed session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the protective measures are closed session and pseudonym today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. What we will do is close the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have now concluded the evidence of a witness who was heard in private. I correctly understand, do I, Ms. Petersen, that there is no other witness available for today or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour, although Chester Stamp is here, and I think he would probably be best situated to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think he'll be very grateful to you for that suggestion. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I -- I think I should indicate to the Court what the position is in relation to the witness. We are now reaching the end of the case. We have called quite a few witnesses. And as, no doubt, Your Honour will have experienced, at this point in time is when we have the witnesses with the greatest difficulties scheduled. We have, for a variety of reasons, including scheduling reasons, withdrawn some from the list in order not to waste time because some of the evidence in relation to those witnesses was marginal. However, there remains some very important witnesses that have presented some difficulties in scheduling, and for that reason we are not in a position to put up any further witnesses this week, and we only have one for next week. After those two witnesses, there are three -- there would be three remaining witnesses that we have not withdrawn from the list. One of them we probably will have to withdraw because he cannot be located or we have not been able to locate him as yet, and the other two were witnesses who had previously been scheduled. Indeed one had been subpoenaed to attend in March or February, that is K87, but who could not attend because of reasons of his health. And another witness Colonel Crosland, who's scheduling presented us with some difficulties in making arrangements for him to attend with the authorities of the United Kingdom. I wish to assure the Court that in respect of these two last witnesses -- or I think they will be the two last witnesses because I don't think we will be able to call the third one, we have done all that is necessary and practicable to get them here as early as possible to testify before the Court. We have been assured by K87 that he will be in a position, having seen his doctors next week, to indicate to us when he would be able to testify. And our assessment is, based on our conversations with him, that he should be able to testify in the week after he sees his doctor. I won't go into his medical problems. I think the return -- the notation on the served subpoena to him from -- just before the Court would indicate the serious nature or the extent of his health situation. So that is on the record. And in respect to the other witness, Colonel Crosland, we have been in very serious discussions with the UK authorities to get him here and the time he will come, when he will come; and having regard to certain inescapable obligations that he has, he has not been able to give us any date earlier than the 26th of October. And that presents a problem, Your Honour, in respect to the scheduling, but we have tried, I can assure the Court, and done everything possible to see if he could be fitted in or brought before. And it is, we are told, the best in the circumstances or the earliest date that can be arranged for him to attend. Your Honour, there is no issue with him in terms of his willingness to come at the present moment; the real issue is when. And this is a witness who -- who has testified before this Tribunal in at least four other major cases, so there is no issue about his cooperation. And I am assured that had it been feasible for him to attend before, he would have done so or would have indicated so to us. I mention this, Your Honour, because I -- I don't think and we have not sought a subpoena for him because he's willing to attend. It's just that we have been told by the UK authorities that this is the earliest date that he can. Those are the reasons for the delay which the Court asks -- well, which the Prosecution asks the Court to accept and understand. I know that we have indicated from the beginning that we do our best to meet the requirement of the Court that we proceed expeditiously and not waste time, and that is why I rise just to indicate what the reasons are for the gaps in the last couple weeks of the Prosecution's case. May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you sit, Mr. Stamp, first you've mentioned the witness K87.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When is it that you expect to know the outcome of his medical examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 29th, 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're hoping to have him available about a week following that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And how long would you anticipate his evidence to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Including cross-examination, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think two days could be reasonably scheduled for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crosland you indicate his availability not until the 26th of October. How long would you expect his evidence to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Two days, Your Honours, I think could be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would then expect to have reached the end of evidence by about the 27th/28th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As I indicated, there might be another witness, but if that witness -- if the issues with that witness cannot be resolved by then, we would be -- we would withdraw that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I be clear, is that the witness you've not been able to locate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- or is there yet a further one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we will learn during next week the position about K87 it seems. I'm sure both Defence counsel and Prosecuting counsel realise that this is introducing an unfortunate delay into the progress of the trial. The Chamber's anxiety is to try and conclude the evidence in this case as quickly as possible. I appreciate that by some standards we have moved with unusual speed given the amount of evidence that has been heard so far, yet by other standards - and especially in the view of the accused - this matter has now gone on for very many months. And clearly it is in his interests if not that of the whole Tribunal to conclude the evidence as quickly as possible. It's not possible at this moment to make precise date orders, but can we indicate that in view of the significance of two of the three witnesses mentioned by Mr. Stamp, that the Chamber feels that it is in the interests of justice that those witnesses give their evidence and that, therefore, the Prosecution should have the opportunity of presenting that evidence. That may mean that we do not finish until close to the end of the month of October the Prosecution case. If that is the way it works out, as seems likely, the Chamber would be aware that it will mean that for most of October both the Prosecution and the Defence will be able to give attention to the next stages of the trial, even though the Prosecution has not formally concluded its case. Therefore, counsel can expect that the moment we conclude the Prosecution evidence, the Chamber will fix a very tight time schedule for the processes that would follow which will have to be followed before we can commence the Defence case, if there is to be one. The Defence will be giving attention, A, to the question of Rule 98 bis, which may or may not commend itself to them. The Defence will be required, of course, to give attention to the provisions of the Rules stating the Defence case, identifying the Defence witnesses, and identifying Defence exhibits, if it is that the Defence is to lead evidence. So what the Chamber is saying now, to avoid any unnecessary waste of time those things ought to be looked at through October even though there may still be one or even two witnesses to give evidence. If I'm correct, the statements of those witnesses have been known, they are available, so that it will be possible for both the Defence and Prosecution to form judgements about these other matters; for the Defence, if it is going that way, to prepare for the eventuality of leading Defence evidence, et cetera, so that it can be expected that we will move quickly in early November through those processes. And should it be that there is evidence to be led by the Defence, that point will be reached well in the course of November and will be underway with Defence evidence if that's the way that it pans out in November. So that I would suggest it will be possible to minimise the loss of time without any undue difficulty and without any unfairness to the Defence so that we can get on with the business of reaching the end of this trial so that a decision can be reached, which is I'm sure where the accused wishes us to go as quickly as possible and which is in the interests of justice and of this Tribunal. With those general words, we can't make specific time scheduling orders now. It certainly may become more possible when we know about the situation of K87, because it seems we can be confident about the dates for Mr. Crosland and it will be possible then to foreshadow a timetable to take us into November; and if we reach that point, to get us to the point of commencing Defence evidence. It, therefore, seems that what we must do now is adjourn with a view to commencing again on Monday with the evidence of the next witness. We will do that. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.28 p.m.,
